questions.question: Which cloud deployment model is owned by a third-party provider and shared across multiple customers?

explanation.correct: Public Cloud is owned by providers like AWS and shared across many customers with logical isolation.
explanation.why: A is dedicated to one org. C mixes public and private. D is shared among organizations with similar needs.

questions.question: A bank stores sensitive data in its own data center but uses AWS for public-facing apps. What deployment model is this?

explanation.correct: Hybrid Cloud combines private and public cloud, allowing data and apps to move between them.
explanation.why: The bank uses both — private for sensitive data, public (AWS) for normal apps.

questions.question: Which cloud service model provides raw infrastructure — servers, storage, networking — that the customer manages?

explanation.correct: IaaS provides raw infrastructure. The customer manages the OS, applications, and data.
explanation.why: SaaS is fully managed. PaaS adds a runtime platform. FaaS is serverless functions.

questions.question: Amazon EC2 is an example of which cloud service model?

explanation.correct: EC2 provides virtual servers (raw compute infrastructure) — a classic IaaS offering.
explanation.why: With EC2 you manage the OS, patches, and applications yourself.

questions.question: Which cloud service model means the customer only manages application code and data — not servers or OS?

explanation.correct: PaaS provides infrastructure plus a runtime platform. Developers deploy code without managing servers.
explanation.why: IaaS requires OS management. SaaS is fully delivered — no code needed. CaaS is container-as-a-service.

questions.question: Gmail is an example of which cloud service model?

explanation.correct: Gmail is a fully managed application delivered over the internet — a classic SaaS offering.
explanation.why: Users only use Gmail — they don't manage servers, OS, or application updates.

questions.question: In the AWS Shared Responsibility Model, who is responsible for patching the OS on an EC2 instance?

options.text: Both AWS and the customer equally

explanation.correct: The customer is responsible for patching the OS on EC2 instances — this is security 'in' the cloud.
explanation.why: AWS manages physical hardware and the hypervisor. OS and above is the customer's responsibility in IaaS.

questions.question: What is a hypervisor?

options.text: A physical server in a data center
Software that manages virtual machines and allocates hardware resources to them

explanation.correct: A hypervisor sits between hardware and VMs, allocating CPU, RAM, and storage to each virtual machine.
explanation.why: VMware ESXi, Hyper-V, KVM, and AWS Nitro are all hypervisors.

questions.question: Without virtualization, what is the relationship between physical servers and operating systems?

options.text: 1 physical server can run unlimited OS instances natively
Multiple physical servers share one OS
The OS manages the hypervisor directly

explanation.correct: Without virtualization, one server runs one OS and one application — highly inefficient.
explanation.why: Virtualization breaks this 1:1 constraint by abstracting hardware through a hypervisor.

questions.question: Which advantage of virtualization directly enables cloud providers to serve many customers from the same physical hardware?

explanation.correct: Multi-tenancy means many customers share the same physical infrastructure securely and in isolation — enabled by virtualization.
explanation.why: Without virtualization-based isolation, sharing hardware between customers would be a major security risk.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a Data Center and the Cloud?

options.text: A data center has more servers than a cloud
A data center is a physical building; the cloud is a delivery model for on-demand, automated resources
The cloud is always more expensive than a data center
A data center can scale instantly; a cloud cannot

explanation.correct: A data center is a physical space. The cloud is a delivery model — on-demand, scalable, pay-as-you-go — that can run on top of data centers.
explanation.why: A private cloud actually lives inside a data center but operates using cloud principles.

questions.question: What does AWS Elastic Beanstalk represent?

options.text: PaaS — you deploy code and AWS manages the infrastructure

explanation.correct: Elastic Beanstalk is PaaS — developers upload code and AWS handles deployment, OS, scaling, and load balancing.
explanation.why: You don't manage servers with Beanstalk — that's the whole point of a platform service.

questions.question: In the Shared Responsibility Model, AWS is responsible for security 'of' the cloud. Which of the following falls under this responsibility?

options.text: Configuring IAM permissions for your users

explanation.correct: Physical data center security — buildings, hardware, networking — is AWS's responsibility as part of 'of the cloud.'
explanation.why: A, B, and D are all customer responsibilities — they are 'in the cloud.'

questions.question: A company is migrating from IaaS (EC2) to PaaS (Elastic Beanstalk). What security responsibility does the company NO LONGER have?

explanation.correct: With PaaS, AWS manages the OS — the customer no longer needs to patch it. This shifts from customer to AWS.
explanation.why: Application code, data encryption, and IAM remain the customer's responsibility even in PaaS.

questions.question: Which type of hypervisor runs directly on physical hardware without requiring a host OS?

explanation.correct: Type 1 bare-metal hypervisors run directly on hardware — no host OS needed. They are faster and used in production and cloud environments.
explanation.why: Type 2 runs on top of an existing OS (like VirtualBox on Windows) — adds overhead, used for dev/test.

questions.question: What is a major disadvantage of virtualization known as the 'noisy neighbor' problem?

options.text: VMs can see each other's network traffic
Multiple VMs competing for the same physical CPU/RAM causes performance degradation
Hypervisors require dedicated hardware for each VM
VMs cannot be moved between physical hosts

explanation.correct: When too many VMs compete for the same physical resources, resource contention causes performance bottlenecks — the 'noisy neighbor' problem.
explanation.why: VM isolation prevents data leakage (A is wrong). Hypervisors share hardware (C is wrong). VMs are portable (D is wrong).

questions.question: Amazon VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) is an example of which type of virtualization?

explanation.correct: VPC is network virtualization — it creates isolated virtual networks on AWS's shared physical network infrastructure.
explanation.why: EC2 is server virtualization. EBS/S3 is storage virtualization. WorkSpaces is desktop virtualization.

questions.question: A government agency needs cloud infrastructure shared only with other government agencies due to strict compliance requirements. Which deployment model is most appropriate?

explanation.correct: Community Cloud is designed for organizations with shared compliance needs — like government agencies with classified requirements.
explanation.why: Public cloud allows anyone. Private cloud is single-org. Hybrid mixes public and private but doesn't restrict to similar organizations.

questions.question: If a physical server hosting 10 EC2 instances (VMs) fails, what happens to those instances?

options.text: They automatically migrate to a healthy host within seconds
They continue running using cached resources
All 10 instances go down — single point of failure
AWS's hypervisor keeps them running without hardware

explanation.correct: This is the single point of failure disadvantage of virtualization — if the physical host fails, all VMs on it go down simultaneously.
explanation.why: Auto-migration (like Live Migration) requires additional high availability configuration — it's not default behavior for all EC2 instances.

questions.question: What is the primary reason virtualization enables faster disaster recovery compared to physical servers?

options.text: VMs are stored in multiple data centers automatically
VM snapshots capture the entire system state and can be restored or moved quickly
The hypervisor replicates data in real time
Physical servers cannot be backed up

explanation.correct: VM snapshots capture the complete system state — OS, data, configuration. Restoring a VM is far faster than rebuilding a physical server.
explanation.why: AWS uses EBS Snapshots and AMIs to enable this capability.

questions.question: A customer enables encryption on their S3 bucket but AWS's physical storage drive is not encrypted by default. Who is responsible for each layer of encryption?

options.text: AWS is responsible for both — they own the infrastructure
Customer is responsible for S3 object encryption; AWS is responsible for physical storage security
Customer is responsible for both since they created the bucket
AWS manages all encryption — customers cannot control it

explanation.correct: The Shared Responsibility Model applies: customer controls data encryption (in the cloud), AWS secures physical hardware (of the cloud).
explanation.why: AWS physically secures data centers, but object-level encryption settings are configured by the customer.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a Private Cloud from a traditional Data Center?

options.text: A private cloud uses shared hardware while a data center uses dedicated hardware
A private cloud is hosted off-premises while a data center is on-premises
A private cloud provides on-demand provisioning and automation on dedicated infrastructure; a data center uses manual provisioning
A data center offers pay-as-you-go billing; a private cloud requires upfront purchase

explanation.correct: A private cloud IS a data center but with cloud-like automation, self-service, and on-demand provisioning layered on top using software like VMware or OpenStack.
explanation.why: The infrastructure is dedicated in both cases — the difference is the operating model (automated vs. manual).

questions.question: AWS Lambda is often called 'serverless.' What cloud service model does it represent, and what does the customer manage?

options.text: PaaS — customer manages only function code and data
SaaS — customer only uses pre-built functions
IaaS — AWS manages functions for the customer

explanation.correct: Lambda is PaaS (serverless variant). Customers write function code only. AWS manages all infrastructure, runtime, scaling, and execution environment.
explanation.why: 'Serverless' doesn't mean no servers exist — it means the customer doesn't manage them. This is the extreme end of PaaS.

questions.question: An attacker exploits a vulnerability in AWS's hypervisor to break out of one VM and access another customer's VM. What type of virtualization risk does this represent, and how common is it?

options.text: Resource contention — very common in shared environments
Hypervisor escape — rare but a known theoretical security risk in virtualization
Multi-tenancy failure — prevents cloud providers from operating
Platform independence attack — caused by running multiple OS types

explanation.correct: Hypervisor escape is a rare but known security risk where an attacker breaks VM isolation by exploiting a hypervisor vulnerability. AWS Nitro's architecture significantly reduces this risk.
explanation.why: This is why AWS invested in the Nitro System — by offloading hypervisor functions to dedicated hardware, attack surface is dramatically reduced.

questions.question: A company uses EC2 for compute (IaaS), Elastic Beanstalk for their web app (PaaS), and WorkMail for email (SaaS). For which service is the company NOT responsible for OS patching?

options.text: All three — AWS always patches the OS
None — the company is always responsible for OS

explanation.correct: For PaaS (Elastic Beanstalk) and SaaS (WorkMail), AWS manages the OS. For IaaS (EC2), the customer is responsible for OS patching.
explanation.why: This demonstrates how the Shared Responsibility Model shifts based on service type — a core exam concept.

questions.question: What is the AWS Nitro System, and why was it built?

options.text: A database service for high-performance workloads
A custom Type 1 bare-metal hypervisor that offloads virtualization functions to dedicated hardware for better performance and security
A network service for connecting on-premises data centers to AWS
A container orchestration service competing with Kubernetes

explanation.correct: AWS Nitro is a custom bare-metal hypervisor that offloads I/O and security functions to dedicated Nitro cards, enabling near bare-metal performance and reducing hypervisor attack surface.
explanation.why: Traditional software hypervisors consume CPU cycles for virtualization overhead. Nitro cards handle this in hardware, freeing up CPU for customer workloads.

questions.question: A startup wants maximum flexibility — they need to run custom kernel modules, install proprietary drivers, and have full OS-level access. Which AWS service and cloud model should they use?

options.text: PaaS — Elastic Beanstalk for easy deployment
IaaS — Amazon EC2 with a custom AMI

explanation.correct: IaaS (EC2) gives full OS access. Custom AMIs allow pre-configured kernels and drivers. This is the only model that allows OS-level customization.
explanation.why: PaaS and SaaS abstract away the OS — you can't install custom kernel modules when you don't control the OS.

questions.question: Storage virtualization in AWS pools physical storage into logical volumes. Which pair of AWS services represents storage virtualization?

explanation.correct: EBS (Elastic Block Store) provides virtual block storage volumes pooled from physical storage. S3 pools distributed physical storage into a single virtual object store.
explanation.why: EC2/Lambda = server/compute. VPC/Route 53 = networking. WorkSpaces/AppStream = desktop virtualization.

questions.question: A company asks: 'If a Type 1 hypervisor runs directly on hardware, and a Type 2 runs on a host OS — which should a cloud provider like AWS use and why?'

options.text: Type 2 — host OS provides better security for customer isolation
Type 1 — direct hardware access reduces overhead, improves performance, and reduces attack surface
Both equally — the choice doesn't matter at cloud scale
Neither — cloud providers use containers instead of hypervisors

explanation.correct: Type 1 is always preferred for production and cloud. Direct hardware access means less latency, no extra OS layer to patch/attack, and better resource efficiency at massive scale.
explanation.why: AWS, VMware vSphere, and Microsoft Hyper-V are all Type 1. VirtualBox (Type 2) is for developer laptops — not data centers.

questions.question: During an AWS certification exam, you encounter this question: 'Which of the following is the customer's responsibility under the AWS Shared Responsibility Model for an Amazon RDS database?' What is the best answer?

options.text: Patching the underlying database engine (e.g., MySQL version updates)
Controlling access to the database via network and IAM policies
Maintaining high availability of the physical host

explanation.correct: For managed services like RDS (PaaS), AWS patches the database engine, manages hardware, and handles HA. The customer is responsible for access control — security groups, IAM policies, and database user permissions.
explanation.why: This is a critical exam trap: RDS is managed, so AWS patches MySQL/PostgreSQL — NOT the customer. But access control always remains with the customer regardless of service type.
